To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
ALS patients show morphological changes in skeletal muscle tissue, which are accompanied by changes in gene expression of markers of regeneration, myogenesis, and inflammation.
the skeletal muscle of ALS patients is in a continuous state of degeneration/regeneration and that the myogenic potential of the patients is limited.
skeletal muscle remodelling is affected in ALS and that the muscle wasting is associated with changes in myogenic potential.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the time course of skeletal muscle remodelling in ALS patients.
the skeletal muscle remodelling process in ALS patients and the myogenic and regenerative potential in this disease.
a detailed investigation of the skeletal muscle remodelling in ALS patients, which is of great importance for understanding the disease and developing new therapies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
skeletal muscle remodelling in ALS patients is a complex process involving multiple pathways and that the myogenic processes are not sufficient to counteract the muscle wasting.
ALS patients show an active muscle degenerative/regenerative process, but this is not sufficient to overcome the denervation and muscle atrophy.
the skeletal muscle is affected at the cellular level in patients with ALS and that this is reflected by the expression of a number of proteins involved in muscle homeostasis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
skeletal muscle is a dynamic organ that is continuously remodelling and that this remodelling is altered in the ALS disease state.
the skeletal muscle is in an active state of remodelling in ALS patients, but the muscle stem cell pool is not able to counterbalance the denervation-induced muscle wasting.

the skeletal muscle of ALS patients is characterised by a progressive denervation and re-innervation process, which is associated with an increased number of atrophic fibres, and a decreased proliferation and differentiation capacity of skeletal muscle stem cell.
The main takeaway from our work is that

skeletal muscle biopsied from ALS patients before and after a period of normal daily activity show changes in markers of neurodegeneration, muscle regeneration, and myogenesis, and that these changes are related to the disease progression.
ALS is a disease with an active denervation/reinnervation process, and that the skeletal muscle stem cells and the myogenic process are affected in ALS.
skeletal muscle in ALS is not only a target of the disease process but is actively involved in the disease progression.
